title: Actors, Sendable & Swift 6 Strict Concurrency
scopeHtml: Scope: Actors, @MainActor, global actors, Sendable, data-race safety, isolation, Swift 6 migration, nonisolated, reentrancy.

notes.title: Baseline and the isolation mental model
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Android you protect shared state with Mutex, synchronized, Dispatchers.Main, limitedParallelism(1) or a single-threaded dispatcher, and the compiler does not check any of it. In iOS (Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 minimum, SwiftUI-first) the compiler proves data-race safety at build time using isolation.

Baseline for every note in this track. Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 target, @Observable, NavigationStack, SwiftData, async/await, actors, Swift Testing, URLSession async APIs, Swift Package Manager. Legacy forms (completion handlers, DispatchQueue, ObservableObject, Combine, XCTest) appear only labelled "old codebases".

The idea. Every piece of mutable state belongs to exactly one isolation domain. A domain is one of: an actor instance, a global actor (such as @MainActor), or "nonisolated" (no protection, so the state must be immutable or Sendable). Code in a domain can touch its state synchronously. Code outside must await, which hops onto the domain's serial executor. Values that cross a domain boundary must be Sendable, meaning safe to share.

   +-------------------+     await (hop)      +--------------------+
   |  @MainActor       | -------------------> |  actor ImageCache  |
   |  UI, view models  | <------------------- |  dictionary state  |
   +-------------------+     Sendable values  +--------------------+
            ^                                           ^
            |  Sendable only                            |
   +-------------------------------------------------------------+
   |  nonisolated async code (cooperative thread pool)           |
   +-------------------------------------------------------------+

Why it matters in production. Before Swift 6, data races were runtime crashes (EXC_BAD_ACCESS on a mutated Dictionary) or silent corruption found only with Thread Sanitizer. Swift 6 turns a large class of them into compile errors. Apple, Point-Free (Swift Composable Architecture), and Airbnb's iOS teams have all published migrations to strict concurrency.

Android iOS
Dispatchers.Main @MainActor
Mutex.withLock { } actor method (implicit lock, async entry)
@Volatile, AtomicInteger Atomic from the Synchronization module (iOS 18, verify), Mutex (iOS 18, verify)
immutable data class struct conforming to Sendable
nothing (convention) compiler-checked Sendable
Dispatchers.Default cooperative thread pool, nonisolated async

Analogy. An isolation domain is a bank branch with one teller window. Customers (callers) queue at the window; they never walk behind the counter and touch the cash drawer.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying an actor is "a thread". It is a serial executor abstraction; the same actor may run on different threads at different times.
  • Saying @MainActor is the same as DispatchQueue.main. Similar effect, but @MainActor is checked by the compiler and can run synchronously when already on the main actor.
  • Assuming Swift 6 changes runtime behavior. The language mode changes diagnostics (warnings to errors), not generated code semantics.

notes.title: Actors: the basics
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Kotlin you write a class with a Mutex and withLock in every method, or confine the state to a single-threaded dispatcher. In Swift you declare actor and the compiler enforces the lock for you.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
actor ImageCache {
    private var storage: [URL: Data] = [:]

    func data(for url: URL) -> Data? {
        storage[url]            // synchronous inside the actor
    }

    func store(_ data: Data, for url: URL) {
        storage[url] = data
    }
}

// Caller must await
let cache = ImageCache()
await cache.store(bytes, for: url)
let hit = await cache.data(for: url)
class ImageCache {
    private val mutex = Mutex()
    private val storage = mutableMapOf<String, ByteArray>()

    suspend fun data(url: String): ByteArray? =
        mutex.withLock { storage[url] }

    suspend fun store(url: String, bytes: ByteArray) =
        mutex.withLock { storage[url] = bytes }
}

Mechanism. An actor is a reference type with a hidden mailbox and a serial executor. A call from outside becomes an async message: the caller suspends, the runtime enqueues a job on the actor's executor, the job runs when the executor is free, then the caller resumes. Unlike a Mutex, nothing blocks a thread while waiting: the waiting caller is suspended, and its thread is freed for other work. This is why the cooperative pool (roughly one thread per CPU core) can serve thousands of actor calls.

What is allowed.

  • Inside the actor, every stored property and method is synchronously accessible.
  • From outside, only methods and properties through await (and only Sendable arguments/results).
  • A let constant of a Sendable type may be read from outside synchronously, because it never changes.
  • Actors cannot inherit from other actors (no subclassing); they can conform to protocols.

Memory. An actor instance is a heap object with a normal reference count (ARC, see the memory note in this track) plus the executor state. Creating millions of actors is cheap but not free; model "one actor per independent piece of shared state", not one per object.

Real examples.

  • Nuke and Kingfisher style image caches and pipelines isolate cache state in an actor or serial queue.
  • ModelActor in SwiftData runs a ModelContext on a background actor (see the SwiftData notes).
  • Apple's own URLSession delegates were historically queue based; new code wraps shared mutable state in an actor.
  • Sentry, Firebase and analytics SDKs use actors or locks for event buffers.

Analogy. An actor is a restaurant kitchen with a single pass window: orders go in, plates come out, and nobody else reaches into the pans.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing actor methods never run concurrently with themselves. They don't run in parallel, but they can interleave at every await (reentrancy, next section).
  • Calling an actor method without await and expecting a warning only; it is a hard error.
  • Expecting an actor to be a faster lock. Hopping has a cost (a context switch to the executor); for a trivial counter an OSAllocatedUnfairLock or Mutex is faster.

notes.title: Actor reentrancy bugs
notes.html:
Android equivalent. With Mutex.withLock, if you call delay() or another suspend function inside the lock, other callers still wait: the lock is held across the suspension. In Swift an actor is reentrant: when an actor method hits await, the actor is released and other messages may run before it resumes. State you read before the await may be stale after it.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
actor Downloader {
    private var inFlight: [URL: Task<Data, Error>] = [:]
    private var cache: [URL: Data] = [:]

    // BUGGY: two callers can both pass the check and both download
    func buggy(_ url: URL) async throws -> Data {
        if let hit = cache[url] { return hit }
        let (data, _) = try await URLSession.shared.data(from: url) // suspension point
        cache[url] = data        // may overwrite a newer value, duplicate work
        return data
    }

    // FIXED: store the in-flight Task synchronously, before any await
    func data(from url: URL) async throws -> Data {
        if let hit = cache[url] { return hit }
        if let task = inFlight[url] { return try await task.value }
        let task = Task { try await URLSession.shared.data(from: url).0 }
        inFlight[url] = task
        defer { inFlight[url] = nil }
        let data = try await task.value
        cache[url] = data
        return data
    }
}
class Downloader {
    private val inFlight = mutableMapOf<String, Deferred<ByteArray>>()
    private val cache = mutableMapOf<String, ByteArray>()
    private val mutex = Mutex()

    suspend fun data(scope: CoroutineScope, url: String): ByteArray {
        val job = mutex.withLock {
            cache[url]?.let { return it }
            inFlight.getOrPut(url) { scope.async { download(url) } }
        }
        return try { job.await().also { mutex.withLock { cache[url] = it } } }
        finally { mutex.withLock { inFlight.remove(url) } }
    }
}

The rule. Treat every await inside an actor as a place where all actor state may have changed. Do check-then-act with no await between check and act, or re-check after the await. The fix above works because inFlight[url] = task runs synchronously in the same turn as the check.

Why Swift chose reentrancy. Non-reentrant actors can deadlock (actor A awaits B while B awaits A). Reentrancy trades deadlock freedom for the need to think about interleaving.

Production pattern. Double-submit bugs: a payment or "like" call made twice, a token refresh running three times in parallel (all three get 401, all three refresh). The standard fix is the in-flight Task pattern: one refresh Task stored in the actor, everyone awaits the same Task. Apple's WWDC "Protect mutable state with Swift actors" covers this exact pitfall.

Analogy. A shared whiteboard in a meeting room. You note a number, step out for coffee (await), and when you come back someone has erased it.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming "actors are like synchronized blocks so check-then-act is safe". Only safe if no await sits between.
  • Forgetting that defer and cleanup also run later, after other messages may have interleaved.
  • Holding invariants across await (e.g. "balance was checked, now deduct"). Re-validate after the suspension.

notes.title: @MainActor and global actors
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Compose/ViewModel you use viewModelScope (Main.immediate) and withContext(Dispatchers.Default) for heavy work; the main thread rule is enforced by StrictMode and runtime exceptions (CalledFromWrongThreadException). In iOS, @MainActor states "this runs on the main actor" and the compiler enforces it.

Global actor. A global actor is an actor with a single shared instance, applied as an annotation: @MainActor is the built-in one. You can define your own:

@globalActor
actor DatabaseActor {
    static let shared = DatabaseActor()
}

@DatabaseActor
final class LocalStore {
    var rows: [Row] = []        // isolated to DatabaseActor
}

Where to put @MainActor.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@MainActor
@Observable
final class ProfileViewModel {
    var name = ""
    var isLoading = false

    private let api: ProfileAPI
    init(api: ProfileAPI) { self.api = api }

    func load() async {
        isLoading = true
        defer { isLoading = false }
        do {
            let profile = try await api.fetchProfile()   // hops off, returns, hops back
            name = profile.name                           // main actor again
        } catch {
            name = "Error"
        }
    }
}
class ProfileViewModel(private val api: ProfileApi) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(ProfileState())
    val state = _state.asStateFlow()

    fun load() = viewModelScope.launch {          // Main.immediate
        _state.update { it.copy(isLoading = true) }
        val profile = runCatching { api.fetchProfile() } // suspend, switches internally
        _state.update { it.copy(name = profile.getOrNull()?.name ?: "Error", isLoading = false) }
    }
}

Facts to know.

  • In SwiftUI, View.body is @MainActor (since the iOS 17 SDK / Xcode 16, View is annotated @MainActor; verify exact SDK behaviour for older Xcode).
  • Annotating a class @MainActor isolates all its members and its initializer. Annotating a protocol requirement or a single method is also possible.
  • Isolation is inherited: a closure created inside a @MainActor function is main-actor isolated; an async method of a main-actor class runs on main unless marked nonisolated.
  • Task { } created inside @MainActor code inherits the actor and priority; Task.detached { } does not.
  • MainActor.run { } and await MainActor.run exist, but prefer annotating the declaration.
  • MainActor.assumeIsolated { } asserts at runtime that you are already on main and traps otherwise (precondition). Use for legacy callbacks you know arrive on main.
  • Xcode 16 has a build setting for default actor isolation (the Swift 6.2 "approachable concurrency" MainActor by default setting, verify for your Xcode version) that makes whole modules main-actor by default, which suits app targets.

What a hop costs. await on a main-actor function from main-actor code does not suspend if already isolated: it is a direct call. A real hop enqueues work on the main run loop, so your code resumes on a later run loop turn. This is why you may see one-frame flicker when ordering assumes "immediately".

Production incidents.

  • "Publishing changes from background threads is not allowed" purple runtime warning in Xcode: a @Published or @State mutated off main. Swift 6 turns this into a compile error.
  • Watchdog kill (0x8badf00d) after a main-actor function did synchronous disk or network work.
  • Main Thread Checker crash in UIKit calls from a background Task.

Analogy. @MainActor is the stage of a theatre: only actors on stage may touch the props; everything else happens backstage and hands props across.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying await always switches threads. It switches isolation, and may or may not change thread.
  • Putting @MainActor on a whole networking layer, which makes JSON decoding run on main.
  • Believing Task { } in viewDidLoad runs off the main thread. It inherits main actor isolation.
  • Forgetting UIKit types (UIView, UIViewController) are already @MainActor in recent SDKs.

notes.title: Sendable: what may cross a boundary
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Kotlin has no such concept; you rely on immutable data class and val by convention, and bugs appear at runtime. In Swift, Sendable is a marker protocol the compiler checks: "values of this type can be safely copied/shared across concurrency domains".

What is Sendable automatically.

  • Value types (structs, enums, tuples) whose stored properties are all Sendable: implicit conformance if the type is non-public.
  • Actors (they protect their own state).
  • Classes that are final, have only immutable (let) Sendable properties, and are not subclassed: can conform.
  • Functions/closures marked @Sendable: cannot capture mutable local state.
  • Basic types: Int, String, URL, Date, UUID, Data, arrays/dictionaries of Sendable elements.
struct User: Sendable {          // public structs need an explicit conformance
    let id: UUID
    var name: String
}

final class Config: Sendable {   // OK: final, immutable
    let baseURL: URL
    init(baseURL: URL) { self.baseURL = baseURL }
}

final class Counter {            // mutable class: NOT Sendable
    var value = 0
}

func run(_ c: Counter) async {
    Task.detached {
        c.value += 1             // Swift 6 error: capture of non-Sendable 'c'
    }
}

Escape hatches, ranked by honesty.

  1. Make it a struct/enum, or make the class final with let properties.
  2. Make it an actor or isolate it to @MainActor (a @MainActor class is implicitly Sendable).
  3. Protect it with a lock yourself and write final class Foo: @unchecked Sendable. You promise safety; the compiler stops checking. Prefer Mutex or OSAllocatedUnfairLock (iOS 16+) around state.
  4. nonisolated(unsafe) var for globals you know are safe, e.g. set once at launch. Use sparingly.
  5. @preconcurrency import SomeLib to downgrade diagnostics from a library you cannot change.

sending parameters (Swift 6). func process(_ x: sending Model) says "the caller gives up this value; it will not use it afterwards", which lets non-Sendable values move across a boundary without copies. This is region-based isolation (SE-0414) and SE-0430. The compiler tracks "regions" of values that can still reach each other, so a fresh non-Sendable object created locally and handed off once is fine.

Real examples.

  • Networking models (Codable structs) are naturally Sendable.
  • NSObject subclasses, UIImage (immutable, annotated Sendable in recent SDKs, verify), NSCache (documented thread safe but not marked Sendable in older SDKs), and DateFormatter are the classic offenders that force @unchecked Sendable or @preconcurrency.
  • Swift Composable Architecture's @Dependency clients are Sendable structs of closures marked @Sendable.

Memory note. Sendable structs are copied on crossing a boundary (copy-on-write for arrays), so sharing a large array is cheap until someone mutates it.

Analogy. Sendable is a sealed, tamper-proof envelope: you may hand it to any department. A non-Sendable object is a live whiteboard: handing it over means two people scribble on it at once.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying @unchecked Sendable makes code safe. It only silences the compiler.
  • Believing every class can be Sendable if properties are let; it must also be final (or a non-open class with no subclassing) and all properties Sendable.
  • Mixing up @Sendable closures (cannot capture mutable vars) with Sendable types.
  • Forgetting that public structs do not get implicit Sendable; you must declare it.

notes.title: nonisolated, isolated parameters and #isolation
notes.html:
Android equivalent. There is nothing similar. The closest is choosing which dispatcher a function runs on with withContext. Swift lets you declare where a function is allowed to run using isolation annotations.

nonisolated. Opt a member out of the surrounding isolation.

actor Account {
    let id: UUID                       // let + Sendable: readable from outside
    private var balance: Decimal = 0

    init(id: UUID) { self.id = id }

    nonisolated var description: String {   // no access to balance
        "Account \(id)"
    }

    func deposit(_ amount: Decimal) { balance += amount }
}

let acct = Account(id: UUID())
print(acct.description)                // no await needed

Use it for computed properties built only from immutable state, for Hashable/Equatable/CustomStringConvertible conformance on actors, and for protocol requirements that are synchronous.

nonisolated async functions (a behaviour change). In Swift 5 mode a nonisolated async method ran on the global cooperative pool. SE-0461 (Swift 6.2, upcoming feature NonisolatedNonsendingByDefault) changes it to run on the caller's actor by default, with @concurrent marking "always hop to the global pool". Verify against your Xcode version; know that this exists because interviewers like it.

isolated parameters. A function can run in the isolation of an argument:

func transfer(amount: Decimal, in account: isolated Account) {
    // synchronous access to account's state, no await inside
}

await transfer(amount: 10, in: someAccount)   // one hop, then everything is sync

This lets you batch many accesses into one hop.

#isolation. Used as a default argument so a generic function inherits the caller's isolation:

func process<T: Sendable>(
    _ work: () async -> T,
    isolation: isolated (any Actor)? = #isolation
) async -> T {
    await work()
}

Standard library APIs such as withTaskGroup and AsyncStream got isolation parameters in Swift 6 to avoid needless hops.

@preconcurrency. On an import (@preconcurrency import Alamofire) it relaxes errors for types in that module into warnings, because the library has not adopted Sendable. On a declaration, it marks your own protocol or API as "adopting concurrency gradually" so old clients keep compiling.

assumeIsolated and delegates. Legacy delegate callbacks (for example CLLocationManagerDelegate) arrive on a known queue but are not annotated. Use MainActor.assumeIsolated { } inside a nonisolated delegate method, or mark the delegate method @MainActor if the SDK declares it so.

final class Loc: NSObject, CLLocationManagerDelegate {
    nonisolated func locationManager(_ m: CLLocationManager, didUpdateLocations l: [CLLocation]) {
        let last = l.last
        Task { @MainActor in self.handle(last) }   // hop explicitly
    }
    @MainActor func handle(_ l: CLLocation?) { /* UI */ }
}

Analogy. nonisolated is a public notice board outside the bank: anyone can read it. isolated parameter is bringing your own teller into the vault and doing many transactions in one visit.

Common interview traps.

  • Using nonisolated on a method that touches actor state; compile error "actor-isolated property cannot be referenced".
  • Assuming nonisolated(unsafe) is the same as nonisolated. The first is a global-variable escape hatch with no checking.
  • Not knowing isolated parameters exist, and writing three awaits where one hop suffices.

notes.title: Swift 6 language mode vs Swift 5 checking levels
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Similar to enabling Kotlin K2, -Werror, or Android Lint "fatal" severity: you ratchet diagnostics up gradually. Swift gives you two independent knobs.

Knob 1: language mode. SWIFT_VERSION build setting = 5 or 6. Swift 6 mode makes data-race diagnostics errors.

Knob 2: strict concurrency checking (SWIFT_STRICT_CONCURRENCY), meaningful in Swift 5 mode:

Setting What it checks
minimal Only code that has already adopted concurrency (annotations present). Default in Swift 5 mode.
targeted Everything that has adopted concurrency, plus checks Sendable conformances you wrote. Warnings.
complete The same checking as Swift 6, but warnings, not errors.

In Package.swift:

// swift-tools-version: 6.0
import PackageDescription

let package = Package(
    name: "Networking",
    targets: [
        .target(
            name: "Networking",
            swiftSettings: [
                .enableUpcomingFeature("InferIsolatedConformances"),   // verify name in your toolchain
                .enableExperimentalFeature("StrictConcurrency")        // Swift 5 mode on older tools
            ]
        )
    ],
    swiftLanguageModes: [.v6]
)

Tools-version 6.0 packages default to Swift 6 mode; use swiftLanguageModes: [.v5] per package to stay on 5 while you migrate.

Per-target migration. Swift 6 mode is set per target, which is why a modular app (see the Xcode and SPM note) migrates leaf modules first.

What Swift 6 mode flags.

  • Non-Sendable values crossing boundaries.
  • Mutable global/static variables (static var shared must be let, @MainActor, or nonisolated(unsafe)).
  • Accessing actor state from the wrong isolation.
  • Capturing non-Sendable state in @Sendable closures or Task { }.

Memory/perf. No runtime cost for the checks themselves. Some runtime assertions come with Swift 6 (dynamic isolation checks inserted when an @MainActor closure is invoked from a non-annotated legacy API), crashing with _dispatch_assert_queue_fail if you lie about isolation. That crash is the signature of a Swift 6 migration done with @preconcurrency imports and an actual off-main callback.

Real examples. Apple migrated its sample code to Swift 6; Point-Free's TCA 1.x has "Swift 6 ready" releases; Airbnb and Square have published notes about enabling complete checking module by module.

Analogy. Minimal is a speed camera on one road; complete is cameras everywhere with warnings; Swift 6 mode starts issuing fines.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing the two knobs: SWIFT_STRICT_CONCURRENCY=complete in Swift 5 mode gives warnings only.
  • Thinking Swift 6 compiler equals Swift 6 language mode. Xcode 16 ships the Swift 6 compiler which compiles Swift 5 mode by default.
  • Expecting Swift 6 mode to find all races: it covers data races, not logic races or reentrancy bugs.

notes.title: Migration strategy and common compiler errors
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Like migrating from RxJava to coroutines or from LiveData to Flow: do it leaf-first, module by module, with the old and new styles coexisting.

Recommended order.

1. Turn on strict-concurrency=complete (warnings) per target; fix nothing yet, count them.
2. Leaf modules first (models, utilities): make types Sendable structs.
3. Annotate UI layer: @MainActor on view models, view controllers already are.
4. Replace shared mutable singletons with actors (or @MainActor statics).
5. Wrap legacy callbacks with continuations / AsyncStream (see the async/await and AsyncSequence notes).
6. Flip target to Swift 6 mode one at a time; keep CI green after each.
7. Remove @preconcurrency and @unchecked Sendable shims as dependencies update.

Common errors and fixes.

Compiler message (paraphrased) Cause Fix
"Main actor-isolated property cannot be referenced from a nonisolated context" Called UI/VM state from a background function Mark the caller @MainActor or await it
"Capture of 'x' with non-sendable type in a @Sendable closure" Task.detached, Task { } off-actor, DispatchQueue.async Make the type Sendable, copy the needed values first, or use sending
"Static property 'shared' is not concurrency-safe because it is nonisolated global shared mutable state" static var singleton static let, @MainActor, or an actor
"Call to main actor-isolated initializer in a synchronous nonisolated context" ViewModel() created in init or a property default Make the owner @MainActor, or create it in .task
"Type does not conform to the Sendable protocol (not final / mutable)" Class with var Struct, actor, or @unchecked Sendable with a lock
"Non-sendable type returned by call to actor-isolated function" Returning a class instance from an actor Return a struct copy or a DTO
"Sending 'x' risks causing data races" Value used after being handed off Don't use it after, or make it Sendable

Delegates and singletons pattern.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@MainActor
final class AppSession {
    static let shared = AppSession()      // OK: main-actor isolated
    private(set) var token: String?
    func update(_ t: String) { token = t }
}

// from an actor or background context
await AppSession.shared.update("abc")
object AppSession {
    @Volatile var token: String? = null
    fun update(t: String) { token = t }
}

Testing. Swift Testing runs tests in parallel and in an unspecified isolation; mark test functions @MainActor when testing main-actor types, or await them:

import Testing

@MainActor
@Test func loadSetsName() async {
    let vm = ProfileViewModel(api: StubAPI())
    await vm.load()
    #expect(vm.name == "Ada")
}

Tooling. Thread Sanitizer (Xcode scheme diagnostics) still catches races in code the compiler cannot see (C, Objective-C, @unchecked types). Instruments' Swift Concurrency template (Tasks and Actors instruments) shows task creation, suspension and actor contention. Hangs appear in Xcode Organizer under Hang Rate, not as crashes.

Real examples. Apple's "Migrate your app to Swift 6" WWDC24 session recommends exactly the leaf-first approach. The swift.org migration guide documents @preconcurrency and sending.

Analogy. Migration is renovating a house room by room with the water still on: finish each room fully before opening the next wall.

Common interview traps.

  • Flipping the whole app to Swift 6 mode in one commit.
  • "Fixing" every error with @unchecked Sendable or nonisolated(unsafe); the interviewer asks how you would verify safety afterwards.
  • Not knowing that Task { } vs Task.detached { } differ in isolation inheritance.
  • Forgetting that third party SDKs (Firebase, Alamofire) may lag; the answer is @preconcurrency import plus tracking updates.

notes.title: Production incident patterns
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Same classes of bug as ConcurrentModificationException, CalledFromWrongThreadException, and double network calls from rapid taps, but surfaced differently.

Pattern 1: Dictionary crash from concurrent mutation. Crash signature in Crashlytics/Organizer: EXC_BAD_ACCESS or swift_retain / swift_release crash inside Dictionary.subscript.setter. Cause: a global cache mutated from several queues. Fix: actor or Mutex.

Pattern 2: Token refresh stampede. N parallel requests all get 401 and all call refresh. Fix: actor holding refreshTask: Task<Token, Error>? (the in-flight Task pattern above).

Pattern 3: UI update off main. Purple warning, intermittent UI glitches, UIKit assertion "Main Thread Checker: UI API called on a background thread". Fix: @MainActor on the type.

Pattern 4: Deadlock from blocking a cooperative thread. Calling DispatchSemaphore.wait() or Thread.sleep inside an async function ties up one of the few cooperative threads; with enough of them the whole pool starves and the app hangs. Swift concurrency assumes forward progress; never block. Use Task.sleep and continuations. Xcode 16 diagnoses some of these.

Pattern 5: Unstructured task leak. Task { } stored nowhere keeps running after the screen is dismissed and retains self until it finishes. Fix: tie work to the view with .task { } modifier (auto-cancelled), or store and cancel the Task in deinit/onDisappear. See the async/await note.

Pattern 6: Watchdog 0x8badf00d. Heavy work on @MainActor. Fix: move work to a nonisolated function or actor, and return only results to main.

Pattern 7: _dispatch_assert_queue_fail after migration. An @MainActor closure invoked from a legacy API off main. Fix: correct the annotation, use MainActor.assumeIsolated only when the API guarantees main.

Interview scenario. "Design a thread-safe in-memory image cache with deduplicated downloads." Answer outline: an actor with [URL: Task<UIImage, Error>] in-flight dictionary plus an NSCache for decoded images (NSCache is thread safe), reentrancy-safe lookup, cancel on memory warning, Sendable result type.

Analogy. Incidents are traffic accidents at an intersection: actors are traffic lights, Sendable is lane markings, and the compiler is the road inspector.

Common interview traps.

  • Offering DispatchQueue.sync as the first answer in a Swift 6 interview. Mention it only as legacy.
  • Saying "just add @MainActor to fix it" without explaining the performance cost.
  • Not distinguishing a data race (memory-unsafe, compiler-checkable) from a race condition (logic ordering, not checkable).

notes.title: Legacy you will meet: queues, locks and callbacks
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Like finding AsyncTask, Handler, and RxJava schedulers in an older codebase.

You will meet these in old codebases. Recognise them and migrate when touched.

// Legacy: serial queue as lock
private let queue = DispatchQueue(label: "cache.queue")
private var storage: [String: Data] = [:]

func get(_ key: String, completion: @escaping (Data?) -> Void) {
    queue.async { completion(self.storage[key]) }
}
Legacy Modern replacement
DispatchQueue.main.async { } await MainActor.run { } or a @MainActor function
serial DispatchQueue guarding state actor
DispatchQueue.global().async Task.detached / nonisolated async function
NSLock, os_unfair_lock OSAllocatedUnfairLock (iOS 16+), Mutex (iOS 18, verify)
@objc delegate callbacks AsyncStream or continuation (see the AsyncSequence note)
dispatch_once-style singletons static let (lazy and thread safe)

Interop. An actor's executor can be a DispatchQueue via DispatchSerialQueue and unownedExecutor for bridging to legacy code (verify API shape before using).

Analogy. Locks and queues are manual gear shifts; actors are the automatic transmission: the same mechanism underneath, far fewer ways to stall the engine.

Common interview traps.

  • Using DispatchQueue.main.sync from main: deadlock, still a classic.
  • Thinking static var singletons are thread safe because Swift initialises statics lazily; initialisation is, mutation is not.
  • Mixing GCD queues and actors without understanding that Swift concurrency does not guarantee executing on a particular queue.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Isolation is the core idea: each mutable value belongs to one actor, the main actor, or nowhere (and then must be immutable or Sendable).
  • Actors serialize access and require await, but they are reentrant: re-validate state after every await, and store in-flight Tasks synchronously to deduplicate work.
  • @MainActor guards UI state; annotate view models and let Task { } inherit it; do heavy work off it.
  • Sendable is the compiler's check for what may cross boundaries. Prefer structs, final immutable classes, actors; use @unchecked Sendable only with a real lock and sending for hand-offs.
  • nonisolated, isolated parameters, #isolation, @preconcurrency tune where code runs and ease legacy interop.
  • Swift 6 language mode turns data-race diagnostics into errors; migrate per target, leaf-first, using SWIFT_STRICT_CONCURRENCY levels.
  • Never block cooperative threads; avoid fixing everything with @unchecked escape hatches.
  • Compare with Kotlin: Mutex and dispatchers are convention, actors and Sendable are compiler-enforced.
